summary: Adds three endpoints to the directory API: a user search by name, a per-key request counter, and an upstream status check.

findings.title: Search query built from request input
findings.problem: Search formats the name query parameter straight into the SQL text. The quotes around the value do not stop a caller from closing the string.
findings.consequence: Any caller of GET /users can run arbitrary SQL against the users database. That caller can read or change every row.
findings.fix: Pass name to QueryContext as a bound parameter instead of formatting it into the query.
findings.suggested_change: rows, err := h.DB.QueryContext(r.Context(), "SELECT id, name FROM users WHERE name = ?", name)

findings.title: Mutex left locked on empty key
findings.problem: Count takes h.mu and then returns early on an empty key without releasing it.
findings.consequence: After one request without a key, every later Count request blocks forever. Each blocked request also holds a goroutine and a connection.
findings.fix: Check the key before taking the lock, or release the lock with defer right after taking it.

findings.title: Response body closed before error check
findings.problem: fetchStatus defers resp.Body.Close before it checks err. When http.Get fails, resp is nil and the deferred call dereferences nil.
findings.consequence: Each request to GET /upstream panics while the upstream is unreachable. The client gets a dropped connection instead of the intended 502.
findings.fix: Move the deferred close below the error check.

findings.title: New handlers have no covering test
findings.problem: The change adds the Search, Count and Upstream handlers. The repository contains no test files that exercise them.
findings.consequence: Tests would have caught the lock leak and the nil dereference. Future regressions in these handlers will also go unnoticed.
findings.fix: Add handler tests that cover an empty key, an unreachable upstream and a quoted search name.

dropped.reason: This hit flags the same formatted query that the c1 finding already raises. Raising it again would report one problem twice.
